q: Under NSCP 2015 Table 103-1, which occupancy category covers structures housing or supporting toxic or explosive substances?
o: Category II, Hazardous Facilities
Category I, Essential Facilities
Category III, Special Occupancy
Category V, Miscellaneous
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Sec. 103 and Table 103-1 Occupancy Category
n: Category II covers facilities whose failure could release toxic or explosive materials. It gets a seismic importance factor of 1.25 (and 1.50 for parts and portions).

q: In earthworks, what is borrow?
o: Soil removed from the site and hauled away
Earth material brought in from another site for use as fill
A level step cut into a slope
Rock left in place under the site
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Earthworks and Foundations), definitions
n: Borrow is soil taken from a borrow pit elsewhere to make up fill. Material dug out and removed is excavation or spoil.

q: What is base shear in seismic design?
o: The shear force in the ground-floor beams
The vertical reaction at each footing
The total design lateral force at the base of the structure
The lateral force on the roof only
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads)
n: Base shear V is the total horizontal earthquake force the structure must resist at its base. It is then distributed up the height as floor forces, largest near the top.

q: In earthworks, what is excavation?
o: The placing of earth material by artificial means
The densifying of fill
The wearing away of ground by water
The removal of earth material
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Earthworks and Foundations), definitions
n: Excavation is digging out earth material. Placing it is fill, densifying it is compaction, and natural wearing away is erosion.

q: What is the story shear at a given level of a building?
o: The sum of the design lateral forces at and above that level
The lateral force applied at that floor level only
The seismic weight of that story alone
The shear carried by the roof-level columns only
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads)
n: Story shear adds up every floor force above the level being checked, so it grows toward the base, where it equals the base shear.

q: Which of these is an Essential Facility (Occupancy Category I) under NSCP 2015?
o: A private garage
A fire station
A retail store
An office building
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Sec. 103 and Table 103-1 Occupancy Category
n: Essential facilities must keep working after a disaster: hospitals, fire and police stations, emergency vehicle garages, designated evacuation centers, aviation control towers and, in the Philippine table, public school buildings. They get the highest seismic importance factor, 1.50.

q: What is the aim of the NSCP seismic provisions?
o: To make sure buildings suffer zero damage in any earthquake
To keep every building fully usable after any earthquake, however strong
To protect life by reducing the risk of collapse and major damage, not to prevent all damage
To stop earthquake ground motion from reaching the building
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads)
n: NSCP 208 states the provisions are meant to safeguard against major failures and loss of life, not to guarantee zero damage or continued function. Some cracking and yielding in a strong quake is expected.

q: Under NSCP 2015 Table 103-1, what is Occupancy Category V?
o: Standard occupancy structures
Special occupancy structures
Hazardous facilities
Miscellaneous structures
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Sec. 103 and Table 103-1 Occupancy Category
n: The five categories are I Essential, II Hazardous, III Special Occupancy, IV Standard Occupancy and V Miscellaneous. Category V covers minor structures such as private garages and sheds.

q: Which lateral system resists lateral forces mainly through the bending of its members and the rigidity of its joints?
o: Moment-resisting frame
Braced frame
Bearing-wall system
Shear wall system
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: A moment frame has rigid beam-column joints, so beams and columns bend to resist sway. It leaves the bays open but is more flexible than braced frames or shear walls.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is a weak story?
o: A story whose lateral stiffness is less than 70% of the story above
A story whose lateral strength is less than 80% of the story above
A story taller than 4 m
A story with no shear walls
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads)
n: A weak story is a strength irregularity (strength < 80% of the story above). A soft story is a stiffness irregularity (stiffness < 70% of the story above). Both concentrate damage, as in ground floors left open for parking.

q: In a building where wind forces are larger than earthquake forces, what applies?
o: The seismic provisions can then be ignored completely
Only the earthquake forces are used, even though wind is larger
Wind governs the strength design, but the seismic detailing requirements still apply
The building needs no lateral-force-resisting system at all
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads)
n: NSCP 208 notes that when wind produces the higher load effects, wind governs strength, but the detailing and limitations of the seismic provisions must still be met so the structure stays ductile in an earthquake.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what impact increase applies to hangers supporting floors and balconies?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 205 Impact Loads (Table of impact increases)
n: The impact increases are 100% for elevator machinery, 20% for light shaft- or motor-driven machinery, 50% for reciprocating machinery and 33% for hangers of floors and balconies.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is a soft story?
o: A story whose lateral stiffness is less than 70% of the story above
A story whose lateral strength is less than 80% of the story above
A story built of timber
A story with a lighter floor finish
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads)
n: A soft story is a stiffness irregularity: less than 70% of the story above (or 80% of the average of the three above). Open ground floors with stiff infilled floors above are the classic case.

q: On which standard are the NSCP 2015 wind load provisions based?
o: ASCE 7-05
ASCE 7-10
UBC 1997
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 207A (Wind Loads, based on ASCE 7-10)
n: NSCP 2015 updated Section 207 from ASCE 7-05 to ASCE 7-10. Wind speeds now come from three Philippine maps by occupancy category, for strength design with a wind load factor of 1.0.

q: For wind design, what is an enclosed building?
o: A building with no windows at all
A building with every wall at least 80% open
A building that does not qualify as open or partially enclosed
A building with a dominant opening on the windward wall
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 207A (Wind Loads, based on ASCE 7-10)
n: Enclosed is defined by elimination: if a building is not open (each wall at least 80% open) and not partially enclosed (a dominant windward opening), it is enclosed.

q: In earthworks, what is bedrock?
o: Compacted fill below a slab
The top layer of organic soil
Crushed rock used as base course
In-place solid rock
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Earthworks and Foundations), definitions
n: Bedrock is rock still in its natural place, whether solid or weathered. Fill, topsoil and base course are all placed or loose materials.

q: What structural element resists lateral forces in its own plane and carries them down to the foundation?
o: Shear wall
Diaphragm
Moment frame
Curtain wall
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: A shear wall is a vertical wall acting like a deep cantilever against lateral load in its plane. The diaphragm (floor or roof) collects the lateral load and delivers it to the walls. A curtain wall carries no structural load.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what impact increase applies to supports of elevator machinery?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 205 Impact Loads (Table of impact increases)
n: Elevator machinery supports are designed for twice the static load (100% increase) because of the sudden starts and stops. Reciprocating machinery gets 50% and light machinery 20%.

q: For wind design, a partially enclosed building has windward-wall openings that exceed the openings in the rest of the envelope by more than what amount?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 207A (Wind Loads, based on ASCE 7-10)
n: A building is partially enclosed when the openings in the windward wall exceed the openings in the rest of the envelope by more than 10%, and also exceed 0.37 m² or 1% of that wall's area, whichever is smaller. Wind then pushes into the building and raises the internal pressure.

q: In earthworks, what is compaction?
o: Removing earth material
Importing soil from another site
Cutting steps into a slope
Densifying fill by mechanical means
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Earthworks and Foundations), definitions
n: Compaction presses out air voids with rollers, rammers or vibrators so fill becomes stronger and settles less. NSCP requires at least 90% of ASTM D1557 maximum density.

q: Why is an impact increase added to machinery loads?
o: Moving or vibrating equipment loads a structure more than its static weight alone
Machinery is lighter than its nameplate weight suggests
Machinery is always placed on the roof, far from the supports
The increase replaces the live load of the machine room
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 205 Impact Loads (Table of impact increases)
n: Starting, stopping and vibration produce dynamic forces above the static weight. The code covers them with a percentage increase on the static load.

q: Movable furniture in a building is normally treated as what kind of load?
o: Dead load
Live load
Wind load
Impact load
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Furniture can be moved or removed, so it is part of the occupancy (live) load. Dead load covers only permanent construction and fixed equipment.

q: How does NSCP 2015 account for the importance of a building in wind design?
o: By multiplying the wind pressure by an importance factor of 1.15
By ignoring occupancy in wind design
By giving separate basic wind speed maps for different occupancy categories
By doubling the wind speed for every category
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 207A (Wind Loads, based on ASCE 7-10)
n: NSCP 2015 dropped the separate wind importance factor of the older code. Instead it gives three wind speed maps with return periods of about 1,700, 700 and 300 years, chosen by occupancy category.

q: Under NSCP 2015 Table 208-1, what seismic importance factor I applies to Essential Facilities?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads), Table 208-1
n: Essential facilities get I = 1.50 and hazardous facilities I = 1.25. Special, standard and miscellaneous occupancies all get I = 1.00.

q: For wind design, when is a building classified as open?
o: When each wall is at least 80% open
When at least one wall has a door
When the roof has vents
When the building has no ceiling
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 207A (Wind Loads, based on ASCE 7-10)
n: A building is open when every wall is at least 80% open (Ao ≥ 0.8Ag). Wind passes through, so there is little internal pressure. Covered courts and sheds are often open buildings.

q: Which of these falls under Special Occupancy (Category III) under NSCP 2015?
o: A hospital with surgery and emergency treatment areas
A building with an assembly room for 1,000 or more people
A private garage attached to a house
A small single-family house on its own lot
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Sec. 103 and Table 103-1 Occupancy Category
n: Category III covers buildings with large crowds or occupants who cannot easily leave: assembly rooms for 1,000 or more, auditoriums, museums and libraries for 300 or more, colleges for 500 or more, jails, churches and power stations. Hospitals are essential (I) and private garages miscellaneous (V).

q: Why are crane loads treated as special loads?
o: Cranes are always removed before the building is occupied
Crane loads are lighter than ordinary floor live loads
A moving crane adds vertical impact, lateral and longitudinal forces as well as its weight
Crane loads act only on the roof deck and never on the frame
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Crane runway beams must resist the lifted load plus impact, sideways forces from the trolley and forces along the rail from braking. NSCP gives separate percentages for each.

q: In earthworks, what is fill?
o: Earth material removed by digging
Rock left in its natural place
The finished surface after grading
Earth material placed by artificial means
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Earthworks and Foundations), definitions
n: Fill is any earth material deposited by people, whether from the site or borrowed. It must be placed in lifts and compacted.

q: What is live load?
o: The load from the use and occupancy of a building, not including dead load
The weight of the structure itself and its permanent finishes
The load from wind and earthquake acting on the building
The weight of fixed service equipment such as tanks and pumps
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Live load covers people, furniture and movable contents. It varies over time, so NSCP gives minimum values per occupancy in Table 205-1.

q: Under NSCP 2015 Table 103-1, what is Occupancy Category IV?
o: Miscellaneous structures
Standard occupancy structures
Special occupancy structures
Essential facilities
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Sec. 103 and Table 103-1 Occupancy Category
n: Category IV is the default for ordinary buildings, such as most offices, residences and stores, that do not fall into Categories I, II, III or V.

q: Which NSCP edition is the 7th edition of Volume 1 (Buildings, Towers and Other Vertical Structures)?
o: NSCP 2010
NSCP 2001
NSCP 2015
NSCP 1992
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, 7th Edition (ASEP)
n: NSCP 2015 is the 7th edition, published by ASEP. It moved wind loads to ASCE 7-10 and concrete to ACI 318-14. The 6th edition was NSCP 2010.

q: How is the weight of a retaining wall itself treated in load calculations?
o: As live load
As wind load
As impact load
As dead load
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: The wall is permanent construction, so its weight is dead load. The soil pressure it holds back is a separate lateral load, H.

q: What is story drift?
o: The horizontal displacement of one floor relative to the floor below
The total sway of the roof measured from the ground
The vertical sag of a floor slab at midspan
The settlement of a footing under the column load
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads)
n: Story drift is the difference in lateral displacement between the top and bottom of a story. NSCP limits it to protect walls, glazing and finishes and to control P-Δ effects.

q: In earthworks, what does "as-graded" mean?
o: The original ground before any work
The surface condition when grading is finished
The level of the water table
The bottom of the footing
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Earthworks and Foundations), definitions
n: As-graded describes the finished ground once grading is complete. Existing grade is the ground before work; finish grade is the final surface after landscaping.

q: Under NSCP 2015, which of these counts as a load?
o: Only gravity forces from the weight of the structure
Only wind and earthquake forces acting sideways
Self-weight, occupancy, environment, settlement and restrained movement
Only the weight of people and their furniture
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: NSCP defines loads broadly: forces from weights, occupancy and environment, plus effects of differential settlement and restrained shrinkage or temperature change.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is structural failure?
o: Only a total collapse of the whole structure
Any visible hairline crack in a slab or wall
Any deflection at all under the applied loads
Any loss of capability that makes it unsafe for its purpose
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Failure is broader than collapse. Failure that only reduces serviceability, such as excessive deflection or cracking that stops the building being used as intended, also counts.

q: What causes the P-Δ effect?
o: Gravity loads acting on a structure that has already swayed sideways
Wind pressure acting on the roof and windward wall
Settlement of one footing more than the others
Shrinkage of the concrete slab as it dries
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads)
n: When a story drifts by Δ, the gravity load P above it now acts off-center and adds a moment P × Δ. That extra moment increases the drift, so P-Δ is a second-order effect of lateral displacement.

q: In common Philippine practice, which concrete hollow block (CHB) thickness is used for load-bearing walls?
o: 100 mm (4 in)
150 mm (6 in)
75 mm (3 in)
200 mm (8 in) only for partitions
ref: Common Philippine CHB practice
n: 150 mm CHB is the usual size for load-bearing and exterior walls, and 100 mm CHB for interior non-load-bearing partitions. This is a practice rule; the actual wall must still be designed for its loads.

q: What is the lateral-force-resisting system of a building?
o: The elements that carry only gravity loads
The roofing and waterproofing system
The elements designed to resist wind and earthquake forces
The foundation drainage system
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: The lateral system, such as moment frames, braced frames or shear walls joined by diaphragms, takes horizontal forces to the foundation. Gravity-only members must still be able to follow the drift.

q: What is the story drift ratio?
o: The story height divided by the building height
The roof drift divided by the base shear
The story shear divided by the story weight
The story drift divided by the story height
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads)
n: Drift ratio = Δ / h. NSCP limits it (for example 0.025 for shorter buildings and 0.020 for taller ones, using the inelastic drift) to control damage.

q: What is a diaphragm in a lateral-force system?
o: A floor or roof that carries lateral loads to the walls and frames
A vertical wall that resists lateral load in its own plane
A diagonal brace that turns a frame into a vertical truss
A thin membrane laid over a roof for waterproofing
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Floor and roof slabs act as diaphragms: they collect the lateral forces at each level and spread them to the shear walls or frames below.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what defines a Type C seismic source?
o: A fault that produces large events (M 7.0 or more) with high activity
A fault that cannot produce large earthquakes (M < 6.5) and has a low rate of activity
Any fault within 2 km of the site
Any fault that is not A or C
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads), Seismic Source Types
n: Type A faults can produce large events (7.0 ≤ M ≤ 8.4) and are highly active, such as the Philippine Fault and the Valley Fault System. Type C faults stay below M 6.5 with low activity. Type B is every fault that is not A or C.

q: Which of these is a Miscellaneous Structure (Category V) under NSCP 2015?
o: A hospital
A large auditorium
A fence taller than 1.5 m
A power station
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Sec. 103 and Table 103-1 Occupancy Category
n: Category V includes private garages, carports, sheds, agricultural buildings and fences over 1.5 m tall, structures whose failure puts few people at risk.

q: Which occupancy category applies to an ordinary office building that is not essential, hazardous, special or miscellaneous?
o: Category III, Special Occupancy
Category I, Essential Facilities
Category V, Miscellaneous
Category IV, Standard Occupancy
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Sec. 103 and Table 103-1 Occupancy Category
n: Standard Occupancy (IV) is the catch-all for ordinary buildings. It takes a seismic importance factor of 1.00.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what defines a Type A seismic source?
o: A fault that can produce large earthquakes (7.0 ≤ M ≤ 8.4) and has a high rate of activity
A fault limited to small earthquakes of M < 6.5 with low activity
Any fault that does not qualify as Type B or Type C
Any fault located more than 15 km from the site
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads), Seismic Source Types
n: Type A is the most dangerous source class, used with near-source factors Na and Nv when a site lies close to it. The Valley Fault System in Metro Manila is a Type A source.

q: In earthworks, what is a bench?
o: A stockpile of borrow material kept beside the site
A relatively level step cut into the ground on which fill may be placed
A retaining wall of stacked stone at the toe of a slope
A trench dug to hold drainage pipes
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Earthworks and Foundations), definitions
n: Before fill is placed on a slope steeper than 1V:5H, the ground is benched (cut into level steps) so the fill keys into it and does not slide.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the NSCP categories of structural failure?
o: Catastrophic failure with loss of life
Failure resulting in extensive property damage
Failure resulting from excessive architectural finishes
Failure resulting in reduced serviceability
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions, Structural Failure
n: NSCP groups failures by their consequence into four categories: catastrophic failure with loss of life, catastrophic failure with no lives endangered, failure causing extensive property damage, and failure causing reduced serviceability.

q: Which structural system relies on walls rather than a complete frame to carry the gravity loads?
o: Moment-resisting frame system
Dual system
Building frame system
Bearing-wall system
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: In a bearing-wall system the walls carry most of the gravity load and also resist lateral load. A building frame system uses a frame for gravity and separate walls or braces for lateral load.

q: In earthworks, what does "earth material" include?
o: Rock, natural soil or fill, or any combination of them
Only the natural topsoil found on the site
Only fill that has been imported from a borrow pit
Only crushed gravel used as base course
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Earthworks and Foundations), definitions
n: NSCP uses earth material for any rock, natural soil or fill, so grading rules apply whatever the ground is made of.

q: Why is the P-Δ effect more critical in tall, flexible buildings?
o: Tall buildings carry no gravity loads in their upper stories
Larger drifts make the gravity loads more eccentric, adding bigger secondary moments
Flexible buildings do not drift under lateral load
Tall buildings never sway, so the effect is theoretical
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads)
n: The added moment is P × Δ. Tall flexible buildings carry large P and sway more, so the effect grows and can lead to instability. NSCP requires it to be checked when the stability coefficient is above 0.10.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what impact increase applies to reciprocating machinery or power-driven units?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 205 Impact Loads (Table of impact increases)
n: Reciprocating machines, such as compressors and piston pumps, vibrate strongly, so their supports take a 50% increase. Light rotating machinery takes only 20%.

q: What is uplift?
o: The downward weight of the roof on its supports
The sideways pressure of soil against a basement wall
The downward settlement of a footing into soft soil
An upward force on floors or foundations from water pressure or wind
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Uplift can come from groundwater under a basement slab (buoyancy) or from wind suction on a light roof. Load combination 0.9D + 1.0W checks that the dead load can hold the structure down.

q: Which discipline covers the analysis and design of structures so they can safely resist their loads?
o: Structural engineering
Geotechnical engineering
Architectural design
Surveying
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Structural engineering deals with the frame and its members. Geotechnical engineering deals with the soil and rock that support them.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what defines a Type B seismic source?
o: A fault that produces only M < 5 events
Any fault that is not Type A or Type C
A fault with the highest activity rate
An offshore fault only
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 208 (Earthquake Loads), Seismic Source Types
n: Type B is defined by elimination: all faults other than Types A and C, typically with magnitudes of about 6.5 to 7.0.

q: Why do helipads need special load consideration?
o: Helicopters are lighter than a crowd of people standing there
Helipads carry no live load when no aircraft is present
Landing aircraft cause dynamic impact loads beyond their static weight
Helipads are always built at ground level, not on roofs
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: A helicopter landing hard exerts an impact well above its weight, so helipads are designed for the aircraft load with an impact factor as well as a uniform live load.

q: Excessive deflection makes a floor unusable, though it does not collapse. Which NSCP failure category is this?
o: Catastrophic failure with loss of life
Catastrophic failure with no lives endangered
Failure resulting in extensive property damage
Failure resulting in reduced serviceability
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions, Structural Failure
n: Serviceability failures, like sagging floors, cracking or vibration that stop a building being used as intended, still count as failure under NSCP, even when nobody is hurt.

q: For a building to be partially enclosed, what else must its windward-wall openings exceed?
o: 0.37 m² or 1% of that wall's area, whichever is smaller
10 m² or 10% of that wall's area, whichever is larger
80% of that wall's area, as for an open building
The total area of the openings in the roof
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 207A (Wind Loads, based on ASCE 7-10)
n: Besides exceeding the other openings by more than 10%, the windward openings must exceed 0.37 m² or 1% of that wall's area, whichever is smaller, and the other openings must be no more than 20% of their walls and roof.

q: Why must roof drainage be designed to prevent water from building up (ponding)?
o: Standing water makes the roof lighter by cooling it
Collected water adds load, and deflection lets even more collect
Ponding only stains the roof and affects its appearance
Water on a flat roof has no weight worth designing for
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Each 25 mm of water weighs about 0.25 kPa. On a flexible roof, water makes it sag, the sag collects more water, and the cycle can cause collapse. Rain and ponding loads are covered in NSCP 205.

q: A structure fails and causes heavy property damage but no one is hurt and it does not collapse. Which NSCP failure category is this?
o: Catastrophic failure with loss of life
Failure resulting in reduced serviceability
Failure resulting in extensive property damage
Catastrophic failure with no lives endangered
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions, Structural Failure
n: NSCP separates failures by consequence. A failure causing extensive property damage, short of collapse, has its own category between catastrophic failure and reduced serviceability.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what impact increase applies to light machinery that is shaft- or motor-driven?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 205 Impact Loads (Table of impact increases)
n: Light rotating machinery vibrates little, so its supports need only a 20% increase. Reciprocating machinery gets 50% and elevator machinery 100%.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what load factor is applied to wind in strength design?
ref: NSCP 2015 Sec. 207A (Wind Loads, based on ASCE 7-10)
n: The NSCP 2015 wind maps give strength-level wind speeds, so the wind load factor is 1.0 in strength design and 0.6 in allowable stress design. Older editions used 1.6 with service-level speeds.

q: A structure collapses and people are killed. Which NSCP failure category is this?
o: Catastrophic failure with no lives endangered
Catastrophic failure with loss of life
Failure resulting in extensive property damage
Failure resulting in reduced serviceability
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions, Structural Failure
n: This is the most severe of the four NSCP failure categories. The next is catastrophic failure in which no lives are endangered, such as a collapse of an empty structure.

q: Which discipline applies soil and rock mechanics to the investigation and design of foundations and earthworks?
o: Structural engineering
Hydraulic engineering
Geotechnical engineering
Transportation engineering
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Earthworks and Foundations), definitions
n: Geotechnical engineers run the borehole investigation, find bearing capacities and settlements, and design earthworks and slopes. NSCP requires a geotechnical study for structures two storeys or higher.

q: What is a permanent load?
o: A load that changes every day
A load that lasts only during construction
A load from an earthquake
A load that changes rarely or only slightly over time
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Permanent loads, mainly dead loads and earth pressure, stay nearly constant for the life of the structure. Variable loads, such as live, wind and seismic loads, come and go.

q: In earthworks, what is erosion?
o: The wearing away of the ground surface by wind or water
The placing of fill in compacted lifts
The removal of rock by drilling and blasting
The densifying of soil with rollers
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Earthworks and Foundations), definitions
n: Erosion washes or blows soil away. NSCP requires cut and fill slopes to be protected from it with cover, drainage or planting.

q: How are fixed interior walls and partitions treated in the loads on a floor?
o: They are ignored
Their weight is added to the dead load
They are treated as wind load
They replace the live load
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Fixed partitions are permanent, so their weight is part of the dead load. Where partitions may be moved later, NSCP asks for a partition allowance (1.0 kPa) on office floors.

q: Which lateral system acts like a vertical truss, using diagonal members to resist lateral forces?
o: Moment-resisting frame
Bearing-wall system
Braced frame
Flat-slab system
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Braced frames resist sway through axial forces in their diagonals, so they are stiff and use little material. Concentric braces meet at the joints; eccentric braces are offset on purpose to add ductility.

q: Under NSCP 2015 Table 103-1, what is Occupancy Category I?
o: Hazardous facilities
Special occupancy structures
Standard occupancy structures
Essential facilities
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Sec. 103 and Table 103-1 Occupancy Category
n: Category I holds the buildings that must work after a disaster, such as hospitals and fire stations, and gets the strictest design (I = 1.50).

q: Under NSCP 2015 Table 103-1, what is Occupancy Category III?
o: Special occupancy structures
Standard occupancy structures
Essential facilities
Miscellaneous structures
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Sec. 103 and Table 103-1 Occupancy Category
n: Category III covers large assembly buildings, colleges with 500 or more occupants, churches, jails and other buildings where many people gather or cannot easily leave.

q: What is dead load?
o: The weight of people and movable furniture
The weight of all permanent construction and fixed service equipment
The force of wind acting on the walls and roof
The loads acting only during construction
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Chapter 2 (Minimum Design Loads), definitions
n: Dead load includes the structure, walls, floors, roofing, finishes, ceilings and fixed equipment. NSCP Table 204-2 lists typical values per area.

q: Under NSCP 2015 Table 103-1, what is Occupancy Category II?
o: Essential facilities
Special occupancy structures
Hazardous facilities
Miscellaneous structures
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Sec. 103 and Table 103-1 Occupancy Category
n: Category II covers structures holding toxic or explosive substances. Their failure could harm people well beyond the building itself.
